 By Annika Rhoades Updated October 27 2026 - 2:23pm , first published 2:19pm By Annika Rhoades Updated October 27 2026 - 2:23pm , first published 2:19pm Save Share Testing found most sunscreen products did not meet SPF claims made on their labels. Photo: Melanie Russell/AAP PHOTOS Sunscreen brands will have to continuously test products after they hit shelves as part of a proposed crackdown on incorrect sun protection factor claims.

 On Tuesday, the Therapeutic Goods Administration announced it was progressing with reforms to strengthen transparency and make regulatory obligations clearer for manufacturers.
 Australia has the highest rates of skin cancer in the world. (Dave Hunt/AAP PHOTOS) Australia has the highest rates of skin cancer in the world, and Choice's director of consumer impact Andy Kelly said changes in sunscreen regulations were critical to ensuring consumer trust.
 ''In a country where around two in three people will be diagnosed with skin cancer in their lifetime, consumers deserve to trust the claims on sunscreen products are accurate," he said.
 Brands are currently only required to provide the administration with SPF testing data upon request.
 The tightened rules would require brands to test finished products, as opposed to just the base formula, provide results to the Therapeutic Goods Administration before being listed, and to continuously test products after listing.
 Labs conducting tests on products available in Australia would also be required to get international accreditation. 
 "This change would greatly improve the transparency around how brands have tested their products," Mr Kelly said.
 ''However, the TGA is not proposing to routinely monitor and evaluate test results."
 A regulatory authority says it wants to strengthen transparency and make obligations clearer. (Lukas Coch/AAP PHOTOS) Test results would only be provided to the Therapeutic Goods Administration confidentially, but Mr Kelly said he believed results should be made publicly available in "the interest of transparency and public safety". 
 The administration should routinely monitor results, while conducting its own compliance testing, he said.
 Other reforms floated would include making clearer distinctions between therapeutic and cosmetic sunscreens, by limiting the SPF claims that cosmetic sunscreens could make.
 The quality and performance of specific ingredients will also be more closely regulated through the development of quality requirements.
 Australian Associated Press
